points: The chapter's metaphor: an abandoned newborn covered in blood is rescued, washed, clothed and raised, and the relationship culminates under the chuppah at Har Sinai. The Jewish people in Egypt had nothing until they were given bris milah and the korban Pesach - clothed not in garments but in mitzvos - and merited redemption.

The ungrateful wife goes astray: Yechezkel alludes to adultery, the third of the capital sins after idolatry and murder. He calls the people worse than Sedom - Sedom hoarded its wealth, but the Jewish people have so much and still do not care for the poor, the orphan and the forsaken.
After all the harsh rebuke, Hashem concludes with a promise: He will never forsake or divorce His people. Despite everything, the bond is permanent.

Rabbi Eliezer stopped this chapter from being read as a haftarah - not because it is harsh, since we read the cheit ha'eigel and many embarrassing passages, but because Yechezkel criticizes who the people ARE, tracing their ancestry to the Emori and the Chiti, as if something is innately broken in them.

Rebuke that attacks identity demoralizes; rebuke that addresses actions motivates. 'You did something wrong' says you can change; 'you are wrong' makes a person shrink and give up. Feedback to children, students and loved ones should target actions, never the person.
